title: Master Hōnen’s Misreading of the Sūtra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Reception by the Buddhas
author: Zhanran
excerpt: The questioner says: the view that “one keeps right mindfulness at the end of life, and the Buddha comes to welcome one” is wrong, while “the Buddha comes to welcome one, and thereby one dwells in right mindfulness” is right. Master Hōnen said: “Moreover, one who truly aspires to rebirth and, trusting in Amitābha’s original vow, recites the Buddha’s name, will have no inverted state at the end of life. Why is this? Because the Buddha’s coming to welcome is itself for the sake of the practitioner’s right mindfulness at the end of life

inline.s: The questioner says: the view that “one keeps right mindfulness at the end of life, and the Buddha comes to welcome one” is wrong, while “the Buddha comes to welcome one, and thereby one dwells in right mindfulness” is right.

Master Hōnen said: “Moreover, one who truly aspires to rebirth and, trusting in Amitābha’s original vow, recites the Buddha’s name, will have no inverted state at the end of life. Why is this? Because the Buddha’s coming to welcome is itself for the sake of the practitioner’s right mindfulness at the end of life. Those who do not understand this principle all suppose that they themselves are mindful at the end of life and that the Buddha comes to welcome them when they recite; a person of this view neither believes in Amitābha’s original vow nor understands the scriptural text. The Sūtra in Praise of the Pure Land says: ‘
Compassion adds its aid, so that the mind is not confused.

’ Because one constantly recites the Buddha’s name in ordinary times, the Buddha will surely come to welcome one; and as soon as one sees the Buddha appear, one dwells in right mindfulness. So let no one think that reciting the Buddha’s name is in vain, or pray only for right mindfulness at the end of life—that is a grave error. Therefore one who believes in Amitābha’s original vow must not harbor doubts about the end of life. For one who first recites the Buddha’s name only at the end of life, Amitābha likewise established his vow of coming to welcome. Those who attain rebirth by reciting at the end of life—the wicked who had no aspiration for rebirth and gave themselves wholly to evil karma—first meet a good teacher’s encouragement at the end of life and then recite the Buddha’s name and attain rebirth; the Contemplation Sūtra says this as well. As for one who has always recited the Buddha’s name, there is no need to insist on discussing the signs at the end of life. Since the Buddha’s coming to welcome is certain, right mindfulness at the end of life is also certain; this principle should be held in mind.” (Collected Writings of Master Hōnen)
Answer:

In this passage Master Hōnen proves his own view by quoting out of context and misreading the scriptural text: “Because one constantly recites the Buddha’s name in ordinary times, the Buddha will surely come to welcome one; and as soon as one sees the Buddha appear, one dwells in right mindfulness.” And he rebukes others: “Those who do not understand this principle all suppose that they themselves are mindful at the end of life and that the Buddha comes to welcome them when they recite; a person of this view neither believes in Amitābha’s original vow nor understands the scriptural text.”
Master Hōnen’s basis is: “The Sūtra in Praise of the Pure Land says: ‘Compassion adds its aid, so that the mind is not confused.’”
Yet in the Sūtra in Praise of the Pure Land (
the Sūtra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Reception by the Buddhas
), the passage “Compassion adds its aid, so that the mind is not confused” reads:

“If there are good men or good women of pure faith who hear the name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life—that name of immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable merit—and the splendors of the merits of the Land of Ultimate Bliss; and having heard it reflect upon it for one day and night, or two or three, or four or five, or six or seven,
with unbroken mindfulness
. Then
(this)
good man or good woman, at the time of death, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, together with his immeasurable host of śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas, surrounding him before and behind,
comes and stands before him
, and with compassion adds his aid,
so that his mind is not confused
. After he has given up his life, he follows the Buddha and the assembly and is born in the pure buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.”
Here the World-Honored One clearly teaches: for the good man or good woman who recites the Buddha’s name with unbroken mindfulness (single-mindedness),

“at the time of death, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, together with his immeasurable host of śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas, comes and stands before him, surrounded before and behind, and with compassion adds his aid, so that his mind is not confused.”
This passage says: because of
unbroken mindfulness
, Amitābha Buddha
comes and stands before him
, and then “with compassion adds his aid,
so that the mind is not confused
Therefore, in this sūtra the World-Honored One teaches:
unbroken mindfulness
the Buddha
surely
comes to welcome.
Yet Master Hōnen, quoting out of context and reversing the logic, misreads the text as: “
Because one constantly recites the Buddha’s name, the Buddha
surely
comes to welcome.

” With ulterior motives he knowingly and willfully twists the scriptural text to deceive the faithful—this is the stock trick of heretical teachings, and Master Hōnen, his disciples and their disciples down to the present-day followers of the Original Vow school, including Master Huijing and Master Jingzong, are all alike in this; see Master Jinghui’s Essentials of the Pure Land School and Master Jingzong’s Master Shandao’s Pure Land Thought, Master Jingzong’s Buddhist Web Interview, and other books, videos, and statements.

Question: Since “this good man or good woman” has already attained unbroken mindfulness, why does the text then say that after Amitābha Buddha comes, he “with compassion adds his aid, so that the mind is not confused”?

Answer: Unbroken mindfulness (single-mindedness) is what evokes the Buddha’s welcome. But this is a shallow level of practice, often not enough to keep the mind undistracted when the four elements disintegrate and suffering presses and maras appear; hence Amitābha Buddha “with compassion adds his aid, so that the mind is not confused.” The Sūtra Praising the Buddhas’ Merit says:
“When life is about to end, with single-minded faith and joy, mindful and never letting go
this is right mindfulness at the end of life, which evokes the Buddha’s welcome
, Amitābha Buddha will
(lead)
the hosts of monks
(the host of śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas)
stand before that person, and maras can never destroy their
(this good man or good woman’s)
mind of right awakening.”
Here, “maras can never destroy their mind of right awakening” is precisely because Amitābha Buddha “with compassion adds his aid, so that the mind is not confused.”
It must be especially pointed out that in
the Sūtra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Reception by the Buddhas
the World-Honored One teaches:
“All you sentient beings should faithfully accept this praise of the inconceivable merits of the buddha-land, the
dharma-gate of reception by all buddhas

Therefore what this sūtra teaches is the dharma-gate of reception by all buddhas (which of course includes Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss), and its core is unbroken mindfulness (single-mindedness). In this sūtra the World-Honored One teaches:
unbroken mindfulness, the Buddha
surely
comes to welcome.
Yet Master Hōnen actually misreads the text as: “
Because one constantly recites the Buddha’s name, the Buddha
surely
comes to welcome.
” This is nothing less than open slander of the Buddha and destruction of the Dharma!
Master Hōnen’s misreadings of sūtras and treatises are everywhere. Let me give just two more examples to show a glimpse:
In the Sūtra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, the Buddha says:

“For the highest grade of the highest rank: if there are sentient beings who aspire to be born in that land and arouse three kinds of mind, they will at once attain rebirth. What are the three? First, the mind of utmost sincerity; second, the profound mind; third, the mind of dedication and aspiration. One who possesses these three minds will surely be born in that land.”

But Master Hōnen says: “One need only know that sentient beings who recite will surely attain rebirth, and they naturally possess the three minds (the mind of utmost sincerity, the profound mind, the mind of dedication and aspiration).” (Master Hōnen’s

Sayings) The sūtra says that one who arouses the three minds (the mind of utmost sincerity, the profound mind, the mind of dedication and aspiration) will surely be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and in the highest grade of the highest rank. Yet Master Hōnen actually reverses this into “sentient beings who recite
will surely attain
rebirth, and thus
naturally possess
the three minds (the mind of utmost sincerity, the profound mind, the mind of dedication and aspiration)”!
In the Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra in Four Fascicles, Master Shandao teaches:
Single-mindedly

reciting Amitābha’s name, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, without regard to how long or short the time, never letting go of the thought—this is called the karma of definite concentration, because it accords with that Buddha’s vow.”

(Translation: Single-mindedly and exclusively reciting Amitābha Buddha’s name, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, regardless of how long or short the time, never letting go of the thought—this is called the karma of definite concentration, because it accords with Amitābha Buddha’s vow.)

[Single-mindedly] In his Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth, Master Tanluan teaches: “single-minded” means thought following thought in unbroken succession, with no other thoughts intermingled. (See Master Tanluan’s Pure Land Teachings.) [Never letting go of the thought] Every thought is Amitābha’s name. [Definite concentration] Correct meditative concentration. When body and mind are pure and free from distraction, it is called “definite concentration.” [Karma] The activity of body, speech, and mind. [Because it accords with that Buddha’s vow] “Single-mindedly and exclusively reciting Amitābha’s name, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, without regard to how long or short the time, never letting go of the thought”—this is because it accords with Amitābha Buddha’s vow. Master Shandao was an emanation of Amitābha; his words are Amitābha Buddha’s words. From this we may know that when sentient beings recite the Buddha’s name single-mindedly and never let go of the thought, this accords with the Buddha’s (Amitābha’s) vow. Scattered-mind recitation of the Buddha’s name, then, goes against the Buddha’s vow!
Master Shandao’s teaching here means:
single-mindedly
reciting the Buddha’s name is the karma of definite concentration, and
single-mindedly
reciting the Buddha’s name is relying on the Buddha’s (Amitābha’s) original vow. Yet Master Hōnen, with ulterior motives,
chopped off the most crucial
“single-mindedly”
two words

, and tampered with it into: “The karma of definite concentration is simply reciting the Buddha’s name; one who recites the name will surely be born, because he relies on the Buddha’s original vow.” (Master Hōnen’s
Sayings)

Question: About practice in the Pure Land school opinions differ widely, and some even say that the true Pure Land school requires no practice at all. Which is right and which wrong, and how should one tell them apart?
Answer: The claim that the Pure Land school requires no practice is utterly wrong. At the end of the Buddha Speaks the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life, the Buddha exhorts: “You should believe and comply,
and practice according to the Dharma
.” In the Sūtra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Reception by the Buddhas, the Buddha again and again exhorts: “
practice as taught
(See
the Commentary on the Sūtra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Reception by the Buddhas

As for how to tell whether the various teachings about Pure Land practice are orthodox or heterodox, one should judge by the principle of “rely on the Dharma, not on the person.” What accords with the words and meaning of the sūtras is orthodox; what does not is heterodox. Grandiloquence that cites no scriptural text is certainly not to be trusted, and even when scripture is cited one must ask whether it is quoted out of context or misread (Master Hōnen, cited above, is one example).
Generally speaking, heterodox teachings have the following traits: 1. They fabricate out of thin air, making things up. (Master Hōnen’s fabricated “Gate of the Vast Vow” is one example; see
Master Hōnen’s Fabrication of the Gate of the Vast Vow

.) 2. They twist and turn, winding this way and that, until people can no longer tell what is the Buddha’s word and what is man’s, and so take fallacy for truth. 3. When citing scripture they misread it by quoting out of context, forcing strained interpretations, and the like (Master Hōnen, cited above, is one example). 4. They use the Buddhist scriptures as their evidence, saying that such-and-such a sūtra says this and that, yet never append the original text.

If you carefully look up the original text, you will find either that it cannot be found at all in the sūtra they name, or that the corresponding original has been deliberately altered by them. These traits, if you observe closely, you will discover.
The Sūtra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Reception by the Buddhas is what the buddhas of the ten directions praise as “
the dharma-gate of reception by all buddhas
—which of course also includes Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. In the sūtra the Buddha says:

“Śāriputra, likewise in the west there are now the Tathāgata Immeasurable Life, the Tathāgata Immeasurable Aggregate, the Tathāgata Immeasurable Light, the Tathāgata Immeasurable Banner, the Tathāgata Great Sovereignty, the Tathāgata Great Light, the Tathāgata Light Flame, the Tathāgata Great Jewel Banner, the Tathāgata Emitting Light, and other such buddhas, numberless as the sands of the Ganges, dwelling in their own buddha-lands in the west. Each of them manifests the mark of the broad and long tongue, covering the three-thousand great thousandfold world, encircling it all around, and speaks these words of truth: All you sentient beings should faithfully accept this ‘praise of the inconceivable merits of the buddha-land,
the dharma-gate of reception by all buddhas

Therefore students of the Pure Land school should follow Amitābha Buddha’s teaching and practice as taught; what accords with the words and meaning of the Sūtra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Reception by the Buddhas is orthodox, and what does not is heterodox.

Question: Master Hōnen says: “That one should ‘attain rebirth by abandoning the scattered mind’ is unreasonable; it is the rebirth of the person who recites with a scattered mind that is the supreme original vow.” (Collected Writings of Master Hōnen, Questions and Answers, “The Question and Answer with Monk Myōhen”) May I ask: is the rebirth of one who recites with a scattered mind really Amitābha Buddha’s supreme original vow?

Answer: Master Hōnen and his followers are masters of twisting and turning, winding this way and that, until people can no longer tell what is the Buddha’s word and what is man’s, and so take fallacy for truth. But there is a simple test: hold the Sūtra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Reception by the Buddhas up as a demon-revealing mirror, and compare their words and deeds with its text, and they will be exposed for what they are. The Sūtra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Reception by the Buddhas is what the buddhas of the ten directions (which of course includes Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss) praise as “the dharma-gate of reception by all buddhas (which of course includes Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)”; that is to say,

the Sūtra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Reception by the Buddhas is the dharma-gate spoken from the golden mouth of our teacher Śākyamuni Buddha and praised and received by Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Therefore this scripture is the fundamental basis of the Pure Land school.
Śākyamuni Buddha teaches in the sūtra:
good men or good women of pure faith
, who hear the name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life—that name of immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable merit—and the splendors of the merits of the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
having heard it, reflect upon it
for one day and night, or two or three, or four or five, or six or seven,
with unbroken mindfulness
Where does it say to recite the Buddha’s name with a scattered mind? Still less does it say that “the rebirth of one who recites with a scattered mind is the supreme original vow”!

[Reflect] To fix the mind on the Buddha and recite his name. The Sūtra of the Original Vows of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva says: “Then the Tathāgata Enlightenment-Flower Samādhi Self-Mastery King addressed the holy woman: ‘When you have finished your offerings, return home early, sit upright, and reflect on my name, and you will know where your mother has been reborn.’ Then the brahmin woman, having paid homage to the Buddha, returned to her house. Because she remembered her mother, she sat upright and called to mind the Tathāgata Enlightenment-Flower Samādhi Self-Mastery King for one day and one night.”
The following is a transcription of this exchange with Master Hōnen:
Question: We sinful, defiled ordinary beings of the evil age of the final era—how shall we escape birth and death?
Answer: Simply recite Namo Amitābha Buddha and aspire to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and you can escape birth and death.
Question: I know the Pure Land teaching is thus. But though I recite the Buddha’s name, my mind is scattered—what is to be done?
[Note: The monk’s question is in fact: How does one attain unbroken mindfulness (single-mindedness)?]
Answer: This Hōnen
(Master Hōnen referring to himself)
likewise finds his strength unequal to it.

[Note: “This Hōnen likewise finds his strength unequal to it” shows that the monk was asking a blind man the way. From this one may also know that Master Hōnen had not attained even the most basic unbroken mindfulness (single-mindedness)—far from having realized the buddha-recitation samādhi that his followers boast of! No wonder Master Hōnen made a great display of preaching scattered-mind buddha-recitation. Consider: when his disciples and the faithful asked him what the state of unbroken mindfulness (single-mindedness) is like and how to attain it, how could he possibly answer? So, for the sake of fame and profit, he simply said: “That one should ‘attain rebirth by abandoning the scattered mind’ is unreasonable! It is the rebirth of one who recites with a scattered mind that is the (supreme) original vow of Amitābha Buddha. This monk’s question, ‘though I recite the Buddha’s name, my mind is scattered—what is to be done?’ is a superfluous matter.”]
Question: Then what is to be done?

Answer: You should know: though the mind is scattered, one who recites the name rides the power of the Buddha’s vow and will surely attain rebirth. In short, reciting the Buddha’s name is the foremost matter.

[Note: “Though the mind is scattered, one who recites the name rides the power of the Buddha’s vow and will surely attain rebirth”—this stands squarely against the unbroken mindfulness of the Sūtra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Reception by the Buddhas (the single-mindedness of the Buddha Speaks the Amitābha Sūtra); it is the saying “one blind man leading many blind men, all pulled together into the pit of fire.”]
Myōhen said: So it is, so it is; it was to hear these very words that I came.
[Note: He came to ask the way, and was fobbed off instead.]

After the monk had withdrawn, the Master said to the monks who were present: Those born in the scattered realm of the desire realm all have scattered minds, just as those born in the human realm have eyes and noses. That one should ‘attain rebirth by abandoning the scattered mind’ is unreasonable! It is the rebirth of one who recites with a scattered mind that is
(Amitābha Buddha’s)
supreme original vow. This monk’s question, ‘though I recite the Buddha’s name, my mind is scattered—what is to be done?’ is a superfluous matter.
[Note: A superfluous matter?!]
Translation:
Monk Myōhen asked: “We sinful, defiled ordinary beings of the evil age of the final era—how can we escape birth and death?”
Master Hōnen answered: “Simply recite Namo Amitābha Buddha and aspire to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and you can escape birth and death.”
Question: “I too know that the Pure Land teaching says this. But though I recite the Buddha’s name, my mind is scattered—what then?”
Answer: “Reciting the Buddha’s name with an undistracted mind—I myself cannot do it either.”
Question: “Then what should be done?”

Answer: “You should know: though the mind is scattered, one who recites the name rides the power of the Buddha’s vow and will surely attain rebirth. In short, reciting the Buddha’s name is the foremost matter.”
Monk Myōhen said: “Yes, yes, it was to hear these very words that I came.”

After Monk Myōhen had withdrawn, Master Hōnen said to the monks present: “Those born in the scattered realm of the desire realm all have scattered minds, just as those born in the human realm have eyes and noses. That one should ‘attain rebirth by abandoning the scattered mind’—there is no such principle! It is the rebirth of one who recites with a scattered mind that is Amitābha Buddha’s supreme original vow. This question of Monk Myōhen’s, ‘though I recite the Buddha’s name, my mind is scattered—what is to be done?’ is utterly superfluous.”
Note:

This question of Monk Myōhen’s, ‘though I recite the Buddha’s name, my mind is scattered—what is to be done?’ is by no means superfluous; it strikes the vital point, for it is the key to whether one attains rebirth or not! Unfortunately, he asked a blind man the way, was taken in by Hōnen, and was pulled along into the pit of fire
. Who knows in which kalpa or which life he will be able to get out again!
Question: It is said that Master Hōnen was a reincarnation of Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva. Is that so?

Answer: Master Hōnen’s heterodox claim that “it is the rebirth of one who recites with a scattered mind that is the (supreme) original vow of Amitābha Buddha” stands in direct opposition to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva’s teaching,
“gather in all six senses, and let pure mindfulness continue without interruption”

—how could he be a reincarnation of Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva? Master Hōnen fabricated the Gate of the Vast Vow and misread the Sūtra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Reception by the Buddhas, which the buddhas of the ten directions (which of course includes Amitābha Buddha) praise and receive—an unpardonable offense; how could he be a reincarnation of Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva? Master Hōnen himself admitted that he had not attained even the most basic single-mindedness, yet his biographies say that he “entered samādhi in this very life”—do you believe it?
These people will dare to fabricate anything!
Still, come to think of it: Master Hōnen dared to fabricate even the Gate of the Vast Vow (
see
Master Hōnen’s Fabrication of the Gate of the Vast Vow

), so what would his disciples and their disciples not dare to fabricate? Master Hōnen dared to misread even the Sūtra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Reception by the Buddhas, which the buddhas of the ten directions (which of course includes Amitābha Buddha) praise and receive (see the beginning of this article); what sūtra or treatise would his disciples and their disciples not dare to misread? In fact, Hōnen himself made his start by reckless fabrication, and master and disciple are one lineage, passed down from generation to generation,
so that reckless fabrication has become the basic hallmark of their teaching

, and the more they fabricate, the more bizarre it becomes (one need only look at Master Huijing’s Essentials of the Pure Land School and Master Jingzong’s Master Shandao’s Pure Land Thought and Master Jingzong’s Buddhist Web Interview), each generation outdoing the one before.
Question: It is said that Master Genkū (that is, Master Hōnen)’s mother, a woman of the Qin family, dreamed that she swallowed a razor and then conceived.
Answer: The great virtuous one Yang Renshan commented: “To dream of swallowing a razor
is the portent of cutting off the noble path
.” (Exposition of the Teaching)
Question: It is said that Master Hōnen was foremost in wisdom. Is that so?

Answer: The principle of the Buddhadharma is that wisdom arises from concentration. Hōnen had not attained even the most basic single-mindedness—what wisdom could he have? Nothing but petty worldly cleverness and argumentation, playing tricks with the consciousness-spirit. “Bodhisattvas fear the cause; sentient beings fear the result.” This means that bodhisattvas, having wisdom, understand cause and effect deeply and therefore fear the cause, planting no evil cause even in their rising thoughts; sentient beings, being foolish, care only for the present, pursue profit and create karma without the least scruple, and only when the retribution appears do they regret it too late. Master Hōnen’s conduct (
having no genuine practice, yet craving fame and gain, he resorted to deceit, cheating others and himself
)—was it not a case of seeking only present fame and profit while ignoring the retribution of the next life? What wisdom is there to speak of! The Sūtra of the Buddha Treasury says:

“Not having attained the way, they say they have attained it; when dead they say they have entered nirvāṇa; people believe and build them stūpas, while they themselves fall into hell. Lay people who break the precepts follow evil monks; for this cause they all rush to the evil paths.”

(Translation: Not having attained the way, they claim to have attained it; plainly dead, they are said to have entered nirvāṇa; people believe and build them stūpas, while they themselves fall into hell. Lay followers who break the precepts blindly follow this evil monk, and for this cause all of them, at the end of life, sink into the evil paths.)

Question: Master Hōnen and his followers preach: recite the name and you will surely be reborn; there is no need to keep the precepts, no need to cultivate merit, no need to purify one’s own mind—it does not even matter if one does evil all one’s life. Is this right?
Answer: In the Sūtra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Reception by the Buddhas, the Buddha says:
“Not by scant roots of goodness can sentient beings attain rebirth in the pure buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.”

This means: one whose roots of goodness (the goodness of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind) are scant cannot attain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Therefore possessing abundant roots of goodness is the foundation of Pure Land study and practice. In this sūtra the Buddha says one should “
keep unbroken mindfulness
,” while these people say that reciting the name surely brings rebirth; in this sūtra the Buddha says “
Not by scant roots of goodness can sentient beings attain rebirth in the pure buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life

,” while these people say there is no need to keep the precepts, no need to cultivate merit, no need to purify one’s own mind, and that it does not even matter if one does evil all one’s life. Would you call these people orthodox or heterodox? Therefore, spoken from the golden mouth of our teacher Śākyamuni Buddha and praised and received by Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss,
the Sūtra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Reception by the Buddhas
is a demon-revealing mirror: at the first comparison they are exposed for what they are.

In fact, if you are interested, you can compare the writings and statements of Master Hōnen and his followers one by one with the Sūtra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Reception by the Buddhas, and you will clearly see whether they are the true Pure Land school, and whether they are the purest Pure Land school!
[Purify one’s own mind] To purify one’s own thoughts and intentions through conscious practice, abandoning evil and cultivating good. The Nirvāṇa Sūtra says:
“Do no evil, practice all that is good, purify one’s own mind—this is the teaching of all buddhas.”
[Roots of goodness] The goodness of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind; because it can produce wondrous fruit, it is called a root.
[Sentient beings] Also called living beings: all creatures that possess consciousness.

As for the “recite the name and you will surely be reborn” that these people preach—is it really so? Does it match the actual facts of past and present? If reciting the name really brought certain rebirth, why would Śākyamuni Buddha have taught unbroken mindfulness in the Sūtra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Reception by the Buddhas, and required those who recite the Buddha’s name to practice as taught, not to give rise to doubt, and not to act with heedlessness? And why would the buddhas of the ten directions (including Amitābha Buddha) praise and receive this dharma-gate of unbroken mindfulness? Therefore
it is not the case that reciting the name surely brings rebirth

. If you believe their heterodox teaching, then, unable to attain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and also failing to keep the precepts, cultivate merit, or purify your own mind—doing evil even to the end of your life—what awaits you
will surely be
the three evil paths, and even the Avīci hell!
Have you ever thought about it?

Question: Then why does the Sūtra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life say that even those who commit the five heinous crimes and the ten evils can attain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss?

Answer: On this point Master Yinguang teaches: “In the Contemplation Sūtra, for one of the five heinous crimes and ten evils who is about to die and whose hell-mark appears, a good teacher (original note: this does not distinguish monk or lay, man or woman; whoever can teach him to recite the Buddha’s name is called a good teacher) teaches him to recite the Buddha’s name, perhaps only ten times, or fewer than ten; he dies at once and, relying on the Buddha’s compassionate power, attains rebirth carrying his karma. These ten thoughts, compared with ten thoughts in ordinary times, differ as heaven from an abyss in their ferocity and urgency, and so he attains rebirth. Pressed by the extreme suffering of hell, as soon as he hears the Buddha’s name he recites it with his whole spirit. Apart from this thought there is no other thought at all. Though he has not personally realized single-mindedness, his mind after all has no other thought whatsoever.” (Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, Third Series, Vol. 2, “Reply to the Lay Buddhist Chen Xinru”) This means that because his ten thoughts at the end of life were utterly sincere and poignant, apart from the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name he had no other thought at all. Though in ordinary times he had not attained unbroken mindfulness (single-mindedness), yet at the moment of death his mind had, after all, no thought whatever other than the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name, and so he could attain rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. As for his roots of goodness: because he repented at the point of death with utter sincerity and poignancy, he could wash away the evil of a whole lifetime—like a deep valley dark for a thousand years, where a single lamp has only to shine and the darkness of a thousand years is wholly dispelled. Therefore
at that moment he already possesses abundant roots of goodness and attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss
. But those who can succeed in this way have been exceedingly few from ancient times to the present—how could one take them as a model? Remember:
single-minded buddha-recitation is the primary practice, and ceasing evil and doing good is the auxiliary practice; neither may be lacking!
Question: “‘Oral invocation’ and ‘mental recollection’ are two different things; only ‘oral invocation of the name’ is the original vow.” Is that so?
Answer: Śākyamuni Buddha teaches in the Sūtra of the Praise of the Pure Land and the Reception by the Buddhas:

“Good men or good women of pure faith who hear the name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life—that name of immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable merit—and the splendors of the merits of the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
having heard it, reflect upon it
for one day and night, or two or three, or four or five, or six or seven,
with unbroken mindfulness
Please note the two words “
reflect
” and the four words “
unbroken mindfulness
Where does it say anything about
an “oral invocation of the name” devoid of “mental recollection”?
Still less does it say that such an “oral invocation of the name” is the original vow!
The Chapter on Perfect Penetration through Buddha-Recitation by Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva
says:
“When a child remembers the mother as the mother remembers the child, mother and child, life after life, are never far apart. If sentient beings
’ minds
remember the Buddha and recite the Buddha, then in this life or in the next they will surely see the Buddha and not be far from the Buddha; without other means the mind will of itself open.”
Please note, in the phrase
“if sentient beings
’ minds”
, the word
“mind.”
It also says:
“Gather in all six senses; let pure mindfulness continue without interruption.”
This means reciting the Buddha’s name with a focused mind and no deluded thoughts.
Master Shandao, in his Four-Fascicle Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra, says:
“As for upright practice: one who, solely relying on the rebirth sūtras, practices this practice is called upright practice. What is this? With a
single mind
he solely recites this Contemplation Sūtra, the Amitabha Sūtra, the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life, and the like; with a
single mind
he solely contemplates, observes, and recollects the twofold adornments of that land. If he bows, then with a
single mind
he solely bows to that Buddha; if he vocalizes, then with a
single mind
he solely calls on that Buddha; if he praises and makes offerings, then with a
single mind
he solely praises and makes offerings. This is called upright.”
Please note the
single-minded, sole calling on that Buddha
— the
“single mind”
two characters; this means to recite the Buddha’s name with a settled, single intent.

The sūtras and treatises above all speak of reciting the Buddha’s name with the thought single and concentrated, not distracted elsewhere. How can one advocate reciting the Buddha’s name with the mouth but not the mind — and even say that reciting with the mouth but not the mind is precisely Amitabha Buddha’s Primal Vow? Regarding how to recite the Buddha’s name, the bodhisattva Awakening Wisdom and Wondrous Practice, who came from the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, instructs in the Direct Pointers to the West:

“The method of upholding the Name must make every word and every sentence, sound and mind, rely upon one another, without the slightest admixture of worldly thought.” “Make the sound accord with the mind, and the mind follow the sound.”
Where is there anything like “‘vocalize’ and ‘think’ are two separate matters, and only ‘vocalizing the name’ is the Primal Vow”?

Question: The Collected Writings of Master Hōnen says: “Question: When the mind is clear, what is the superiority or inferiority of the recitation done then, compared with recitation amid deluded thought? Answer: The merit is exactly equal, with no difference.” Are these two kinds of recitation truly equal in merit, with no difference?

Answer: This fully shows that Master Hōnen never attained recitation with a clear mind and never experienced the vast difference between ‘recitation when the mind is clear’ and ‘recitation amid deluded thought’ — only then could he utter such ignorant words as ‘the merit is exactly equal, with no difference.’

When the mind is clear, one recites and the water is clear and the moon appears — the resonance and the response meet and communicate (ganying dao jiao). This is the stage of which the Pure Land patriarchs said, ‘One thought in correspondence, one Buddha; every thought in correspondence, one Buddha.’ Therefore the Buddha teaches us to be mindful without confusion (one mind undisturbed), in order to ensure rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Master Hōnen, however, says that ‘the merit of recitation when the mind is clear and of recitation amid deluded thought is exactly equal, with no difference.’ This runs against the principle of the Buddha’s Dharma, and is a negation of
the Sūtra in Praise of the Pure Land, the Buddha’s Reception
where it says
“mindfulness without confusion... practice as taught
, and be born in that Buddha land
and a negation of the very method that Amitabha Buddha praised and received.
How heretical it is — this is clear!
Master Hōnen has
never in all his life attained recitation with a clear mind — to say nothing of mindfulness without confusion (one mind undisturbed)! Is such a person fit to be a patriarch of the Pure Land school?

[Merit] Virtue means attainment; what is attained through the merit of cultivation is therefore called merit and virtue. [The water is clear and the moon appears] The mind of sentient beings is like water, and Amitabha Buddha is like the moon. When the water of the mind is clear (still and clear), the Buddha-moon appears; when the water of the mind is roiled and turbid (stirred and turbid), the Buddha-moon shines, yet its reflection is not distinctly seen. [Resonance and response meeting across] The resonance of sentient beings and the response of Amitabha Buddha mutually communicate.
[Mindfulness without confusion
practice as taught, and be born in that Buddha land] In the Sūtra in Praise of the Pure Land, the Buddha’s Reception, the Buddha says:

“Sāriputra, if virtuous men or virtuous women of pure faith hear such a name of Immeasurable Life Buddha, of his immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable merit and virtue, along with the merit, virtue, and adornment of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and having heard, reflect upon it — whether for one day and night, or two, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven,
being mindful without confusion

. Then, whether it be a virtuous man or a virtuous woman, at the end of life, Immeasurable Life Buddha, together with his immeasurable host of śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas, with their retinue before and behind, comes and stands before them, and with compassion protects and aids them, causing the mind not to be confused. Having relinquished their lives, they follow the Buddha’s assembly and are reborn in the pure Buddha land of Immeasurable Life, the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Moreover, Sāriputra, observing this great matter of benefit, bliss, and ease, I speak true and sincere words: if virtuous men or virtuous women of pure faith hear such inconceivable merit and virtue of the name of Immeasurable Life Buddha and of his pure Buddha land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, they should all believe and receive it, and arouse the vow,
and practice as taught
, and be born in that Buddha land
Please note:
“practice as taught
, and be born in that Buddha land
Consider: if it were truly that ‘recitation when the mind is clear and recitation amid deluded thought have merit exactly equal
, with no difference’

, and truly that ‘calling the name guarantees rebirth,’ then why should our teacher Śākyamuni Buddha, in the Sūtra in Praise of the Pure Land, the Buddha’s Reception, require those who recite the Buddha’s name to attain mindfulness without confusion, and repeatedly enjoin
‘diligently and earnestly practice as taught, and harbor no doubt’
‘with deep mind believe and understand, arouse the vow and be reborn, and do not practice laxity’
? Why would the Buddhas of the ten directions (including Amitabha Buddha) praise and receive this method of mindfulness without confusion?
Reciting the Buddha’s name with a single mind
(recitation with a clear mind)
is supremely wondrous:
For,
reciting the Buddha’s name with a single mind, the three studies of precepts, meditation, and wisdom are all complete.
Great Master Lianchi says:
“Precepts have the meaning of preventing wrong; if one can
recite the Buddha’s name with a single mind
, all evils dare not enter — this is precepts. Meditation has the meaning of removing scattering; if one
recites the Buddha’s name with a single mind
, the mind does not turn to other objects
(the mind does not cling to anything else)

— this is meditation. Wisdom has the meaning of clear illumination; if one observes the sound of the Buddha’s name so that every word is distinct, and also observes that the one who recites and the recitation are both unobtainable — this is wisdom. To recite the Buddha’s name thus is precepts, meditation, and wisdom.”
The Collected Sayings of the Yunqi Pure Land

Translation: Precepts mean to prevent and forbid wrong; if one is able to recite the Buddha’s name with a single mind, all evils dare not enter — this is precepts. Meditation means to remove scattering; if one recites the Buddha’s name with a single mind,
the mind does not cling to anything else

— this is meditation. Wisdom means clear illumination; if one contemplates the Buddha’s name so that every word is distinct, and also observes that the one who recites and the recitation are both unobtainable — this is wisdom. To recite the Buddha’s name thus is precepts, meditation, and wisdom
indeed!
For, reciting the Buddha’s name with a single mind, the six pāramitās and the myriad practices are all complete.
Great Master Lianchi says:
“Now,
reciting the Buddha’s name with a single mind,
the myriad conditions are naturally relinquished — this is the pāramitā of giving;
reciting the Buddha’s name with a single mind,
all evils naturally cease — this is the pāramitā of precepts;
reciting the Buddha’s name with a single mind,
the mind naturally becomes gentle — this is the pāramitā of patience;
reciting the Buddha’s name with a single mind,
never falling back — this is the pāramitā of diligence;
reciting the Buddha’s name with a single mind,
other thoughts not arising — this is the pāramitā of meditation
reciting the Buddha’s name with a single mind,
right mindfulness clear and distinct — this is the pāramitā of prajñā.
Extending this to the utmost,
it does not go beyond the single mind
(that is, reciting the Buddha’s name with a single mind)
— the myriad practices are all complete.”
(The Commentaries on the Amitabha Sūtra)

Translation: Now, reciting the Buddha’s name with a single mind, the myriad conditions are naturally relinquished — this is the pāramitā of giving; reciting with a single mind, all evils naturally cease — this is the pāramitā of precepts; reciting with a single mind, the mind naturally becomes gentle — this is the pāramitā of patience; reciting with a single mind, never falling back — this is the pāramitā of diligence; reciting with a single mind, no other thoughts arising — this is the pāramitā of meditation; reciting with a single mind, right mindfulness clear and distinct — this is the pāramitā of prajñā. Extending this to all practices, reciting the Buddha’s name with a single mind, the myriad practices are all complete.

[Myriad practices] All the practices. The Treatise on the Bodhi Mind says: ‘Passing through three asamkhya kalpas, cultivating the six pāramitās and the myriad practices, all fully complete, one then realizes Buddhahood.’
Therefore,
reciting the Buddha’s name with a single mind

is the great bliss, the great liberation. Letting go of the myriad conditions and reciting the Buddha’s name with a single mind, one gains great freedom. Entering this realm, one then knows its flavor. When has Master Hōnen ever tasted so much as a trace of the flavor of the Dharma?

Master Hōnen and his followers go against the meaning of the scriptures, distort the scriptural text, and slander the Buddha and the Dharma as they preach. This is impure preaching. Those who preach impurely have extremely heavy karmic offenses
(more than if one took the lives of all the sentient beings in the three-thousand great-thousand world)
, and their retribution is extremely frightful
(they fall into the great hells)
, and the fate of their followers is also extremely pitiable
(having entered false views from which it is hard to return, they suffer decline and misery for hundreds of thousands of eons, with ceaseless hardship)
. The Buddha says:
“Sāriputra, though the enemy may take life
(though the bandit-enemy is vicious and takes one’s life)
, it is only the loss of one body
(but the life that is taken is only this single lifetime)
; such a foolish person
who preaches impurely
, for thousands of billions of eons causes great decline and misery to sentient beings
(because false views have entered their hearts, from life to life, for thousands of billions of eons, they can hardly escape, and calamities follow one upon another)
. Such a person
(the person deluded by impure preaching)

— stupid and dark — covers the Buddha’s bodhi mind of its origin, greed and clinging blaze up again and again, continuing without cease; because of greed and clinging, they wander through the five destinies, with no good path, and birth and death do not end. Therefore, Sāriputra,
one who preaches impurely commits extremely many offenses, also acts as an evil knowing one for sentient beings, and also slanders the Buddhas of the past, the future, and the present
. Sāriputra, setting aside the sentient beings of this Jambudvīpa,
if a person were to take the lives of all the sentient beings in the three-thousand great-thousand world, the offense of impure preaching is greater than this
. Why? Such a person ruins the anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all the Buddhas, and abets the work of Māra,
and also causes sentient beings to suffer decline and misery for hundreds of thousands of eons
; it can only bind and cannot untie. Know that such a person is an evil knowing one to sentient beings, and by such false speech slanders all the Buddhas before the great assembly,
and for this cause falls into the great hells
Therefore know that
such a person would rather cut out his own tongue with a sharp knife than preach impurely in the midst of the assembly
(The Buddha Repository Sūtra)

[Five destinies] Heaven, humans, hells, hungry ghosts, and animals. If one speaks of six destinies, the asuras are added. The fifth is not mentioned here because the asura realm is included within the destinies of heaven, humans, animals, and hungry ghosts.
